proves: vertical alignment moves the whole paragraph within the box that holds it, by the amount the box has left over. The property was resolved and then read by nothing - not by measure, not by layout, not by paint - until this fixture's commit.
checkable: 280x88, three 80x72 grey cells at y=8..79, at x=8, 96 and 184, each holding the word Hxgp at 18px in the Fixture family. The ink is 18 rows tall in every cell. Read the first and last row carrying ink darker than 120 in the red channel: cell 0 (Top) is rows 14 to 31, cell 1 (Middle) is rows 37 to 54, cell 2 (Bottom) is rows 59 to 76. Same glyphs, same height, three positions.
checkable_horizontally: the ink spans x+1 to x+31 in every cell - 9..39, 97..127, 185..215 - because the property moves the paragraph on one axis only. Worth reading as well as the rows: a change that moved the text on both axes would satisfy every row measurement above and be wrong.
expected: Top leaves the paragraph where the baseline puts it. Middle adds half the leftover space and Bottom adds all of it. Not clamped at zero, which is v1's behaviour too: a paragraph taller than its box hangs out of it rather than being pinned to the top.
why_the_boxes_are_taller_than_the_text: the property moves the paragraph by what the box has left over, and a text node sized to its own content has nothing left over - so all three alignments agree exactly where a fixture is easiest to write. A control pair built that way reported this property as dead after its first control mistake had already been fixed, which is how the second one was found.
which_cell_is_the_control: cell 0. Top is the default and every other text fixture in this suite is already drawing it, so a change that moved Top would move them too - the control's job here is to hold still while the other two move.
not_css_vertical_align: CSS places one inline box on its line; this places the whole paragraph in the node's box, which is what v1 does and what a scene with one paragraph per node can express. Where v2 and v1 disagree on what is drawn, v1 wins.
status: measured from the committed image. Vertical alignment landed in the commit that added this fixture. All three cells reading rows 14 to 31 again is the regression it exists to catch - that is what the property being ignored looks like.
chrome: the ink row spans are Chrome's, not ours: [[14,31],[37,54],[60,77]], and ours are identical. Scene: three 80x72 cells holding one word at 18px, aligned top, middle and bottom. Measured by rendering the equivalent CSS in Chrome and reading its own painted bytes.
the-threshold-is-part-of-the-measurement: ink means a channel below 128, and the cell backgrounds are white or near it. Both halves matter. The first reading of these spans used a threshold of 200 and reported Chrome one row longer at the foot of every span - the faintest antialiased row, which this renderer puts one shade lighter. At 240 the #eee cell background of vertical-align counts as ink and the three cells become one span from y=8 to y=79. An ink-span comparison without a stated threshold is not a measurement, and a threshold close to the background is not one either.
what-moved-when-text-left-the-paragraph: this image changed by under a pixel per line when text moved off SkParagraph onto line boxes computed here. The cause is the strut: Chrome rounds fontBoundingBoxAscent and descent to whole pixels, 19 and 5 at 16px, where the face reports 19.088 and 4.624 - so an unrounded pair makes every line box 0.288 short and the error accumulates down a paragraph. crates/meo-canvas-core/tests/chrome_text_truth.rs pins that and the line-box arithmetic around it.
